proposed_title: Would Falling From Space Make You Hit the Ground Faster?
recommended_slot: Day 1 (launch day = day the video is actually ready)
q1_understandable: Yes. "From space" must be defined on screen: dropped at rest from 100 km, ignoring re-entry heating and orbital speed.
q2_whatif_fit: Yes: classic counter-intuitive what-if with a numeric answer.
q3_promise_vs_supportable_answer: Supported by my model: landing speed is the same from 1 km and 100 km (about 204 km/h at the prior CdA/m 0.00505; 185 and 164 km/h at CdA 0.55 and 0.7 m2 for 90 kg), while peak speed differs (model 3,630 km/h from 100 km, model-only). Title asks "faster"; honest answer is "no, about the same landing speed". Never say survivable.
q5_overlap_adjacent_uploads: Close premise exists: Quiet World "POV: You Fall From Every Height" (1 m to edge of space) 51K views in 8 days; keep the single-question comparison (landing vs peak) as the distinct angle.
revised_title_options: 1) Do You Hit the Ground Faster If You Fall From Space? | 2) Fall From 1 km or From Space: Which Lands Faster?
thumbnail_concept: Two identical figures marked 1 km and 100 km above one shared speed dial reading about the same value; a faint ghost arrow shows the much higher peak. One number on screen only.
opening_direction_15_30s: State the exact setup (same body, same pose, windless, dropped at rest from 1 km and from 100 km). Show both speed curves leaving together then crossing before the ground; promise: one number is the same and one is not. Define "space" and the model limits before any claim.
competition_and_topic_fit: Crowded: 14 near-premise uploads in the last 30 d (13 of them under 1K views); but a 140-sub channel got 51K in 8 d on the close premise and a 26-day-old "What If You Fell From Space?" has 18.7K. Fit high.
science_readiness: READY WITH CAVEATS (state posture/CdA, range 164-205 km/h). The 100 km peak speed and any hypersonic drag claim: HOLD FOR SCIENCE.
production_dependency: Script v3 approved 2026-11-19, fact-check and thumbnail exist (REPORTED by earlier audits, files not opened by me). No record the video is finished.
counterargument: Search for the exact idea is dominated by Baumgartner/Red Bull footage (89M-158M); a near-identical 8-day-old video shows copying risk and may make this look derivative.
position_rationale: Reasonable first slot only if finished: ready, evergreen, strongest recent small-channel signal in the set. If not ready, Day 1 is the first ready item (do not publish unfinished).

proposed_title: Why Do You Slow Down Before Hitting the Ground?
parent_relation: After parent: it is the detail "peak then slow", so it cannot spoil the long and reads as its follow-up. It is derivative, not an independent test.
q1_understandable: Partly. A viewer may think "I do not slow down, I speed up". The first 3 s must say "from high up".
q3_promise_vs_supportable_answer: True only for falls from above roughly 5 km: model peak vs landing 248 vs 204 km/h from 5 km, 321 vs 204 from 10 km, 1,366 vs 204 from 39 km; from 1 km there is no slow-down (205 vs 204).
q4_short_standalone_payoff: Yes: premise (high fall peaks) + reason (air gets thicker, drag grows with speed squared) + number pair, in under 45 s, without the long.
q5_overlap_adjacent_uploads: Overlaps P1 by design; must not repeat P1 visuals one-to-one.
revised_title_options: 1) Why Does a Fall From Space Slow Down Before You Land? | 2) Falling From High Up: Why Your Speed Drops Before the Ground

opening_direction_15_30s: Open on the hump: from 1 km you never slow; from 39 km you peak near 1,370 km/h then drop to about 200. Ask why, answer with thickening air and drag, close on the two numbers.
competition_and_topic_fit: Exact question not found as a strong video (7 keyword-near hits, top are textbook terminal-velocity lessons 109K-235K); topic fit medium.
science_readiness: READY WITH CAVEATS (altitude threshold is model-dependent).
production_dependency: No script exists for this reworded Short (earlier draft v1 was "excerpt" version, REPORTED).
counterargument: It is the same answer as P1 re-cut; if P1 underperforms the Short has no independent reach.

proposed_title: Could You Jump Into Orbit Around a Tiny Planet?
q1_understandable: Yes. Needs a stated radius and density in the first 10 s.
q2_whatif_fit: Yes: strong visual what-if with a computable boundary.
q3_promise_vs_supportable_answer: Supported with nuance: at rho 2,700 kg/m3 a 3 m/s horizontal jump needs R about 3.5 km (2.4 km at rho 5,514; 4.1 km at 1,900), orbit period 84-144 min. A horizontal launch from the surface returns to the launch point after one period (grazing orbit): say "orbit" only with this explanation; ignores terrain, rotation, tides, and that real jumps are not 3 m/s horizontal.
q5_overlap_adjacent_uploads: Follows P1 (different family: scale/POV vs falling). Question-level overlap with the printed xkcd chapter "Little Planet" pp. 117-121 (REPORTED by earlier audit; book text not read); distinct treatment = radius/density table and return-to-footprints timeline, no copied art or jokes.
revised_title_options: 1) Could You Jump Into Orbit Around a Tiny Planet? (keep) | 2) How Small Must a Planet Be to Jump Into Orbit?
thumbnail_concept: Figure mid-leap above a small sphere, a dotted loop returns to the footprints; text: "ORBIT BY JUMPING?".
opening_direction_15_30s: Stand on a stated tiny sphere (radius and density shown), jump sideways at 3 m/s, trace the path: it curves with the ground. Ask what radius makes that a full loop; promise a table by density and the twist that you land in your own footprints.

proposed_title: What If the Moon Vanished Tonight?
decision: KEEP WITH REVISED TITLE / ANGLE (low-medium confidence) + MOVE
q2_whatif_fit: Yes, the most conventional what-if in the set.
q3_promise_vs_supportable_answer: Tides: supported (solar tide-generating force is 0.46 of lunar; solar-only share about 31% of the combined strength, basin response not modelled). Tilt/climate: unsettled between Laskar 1993 and Lissauer et al. 2012 (full text not read by me). "Hour by hour" or million-year timelines overpromise. Mass disappearing violates conservation: label as hypothetical.
q5_overlap_adjacent_uploads: Next to P7 tides Short: split content (long = night sky, tides, tilt uncertainty; Short = tides only).
revised_title_options: 1) If the Moon Vanished Tonight, What Changes First? | 2) The Moon Vanishes: What Changes Tonight and What Takes Millions of Years
thumbnail_concept: Night sky with an empty dashed Moon circle and a single ocean line; text: "TONIGHT".
opening_direction_15_30s: Start at moonset: the circle is empty; list the three things we can compute (light, tides, orbit unchanged) before the one we cannot (tilt). Promise separation of computed vs uncertain.
competition_and_topic_fit: Most copied exact title: 29 near-premise uploads in 30 d (21 with "Moon Disappeared/Vanished Tonight/Tomorrow" titles, 20 of those under 1K views); older 1-4M kid-channel videos (AumSum 3.6M, Insider Tech 1.7M, What If 1.2M). xkcd official has not made Moon-vanishes (it made Moon black hole, electrons, pool, laser).

counterargument: Large old view counts prove broad demand; many tiny copies may not hurt a well-made video, so replacing it (my earlier view) may be too harsh. Codex 2 preferred a narrowed one-coast tide counterfactual.

science_readiness: HOLD FOR SCIENCE (define what stops and for how long).
position_rationale: Weak backup: highest overlap in the set.
